mcq.q: When is a plain parallel workflow better than a coordinator agent?
options: When the decomposition can be written in code
mcq.why: If you know the split, code is cheaper and more predictable.

mcq.q: Choose all the conditions under which multiple agents help.
options: The subtasks are tightly coupled and short
The task needs more material than fits in one context
Subtasks need different tools or permissions
An independent reviewer with fresh context is useful
mcq.why: Breadth, separable expertise, independent verification and organisational boundaries justify multiple agents.
distractors: Tightly coupled, short tasks are where multiple agents do not help.

mcq.q: Published reports on research agents describe multi-agent systems using how many tokens compared with single-agent chat?
options: Several times to an order of magnitude more
mcq.why: Parallel workers each read and summarise, so token use grows a lot.
distractors: The reported range is much wider.
Workers add briefs, summaries and synthesis.

mcq.q: Why does a single agent fail the chapter's Q3 complaints example?
options: It would exhaust its context on the first of three sources (about 40,000 records)
It is not allowed to read tickets
mcq.why: Breadth exceeds one context, so workers read parts and return condensed findings.
distractors: Start-up time is not the problem.

mcq.q: Mixing billing tools and identity tools in one agent's prompt tends to…
mcq.why: Separable tools and permissions are a reason to split agents.

mcq.q: Why does independent verification need a separate reviewer?
options: Two agents always agree on the truth
The reviewer is always a bigger model
A fresh context catches errors the producer is blind to
mcq.why: A reviewer that shares the producer's context shares its blind spots.
distractors: Agreement is not proof, especially from the same source.
Model size is not the point.

mcq.q: Three agents agree on an answer, but all read the same outdated document. What does the agreement show?
options: Little; they share the same wrong source
mcq.why: Agreement between agents with the same evidence is not independent validation.
distractors: Agreement from one source is not independent.
This is exactly when verification is needed.

mcq.q: Each worker in the example returns a 300-word summary with evidence IDs. Why not return raw records?
options: To protect the coordinator's context and keep the result traceable
mcq.why: Condensed findings with evidence let the coordinator synthesise without overflowing.
distractors: They can, but they would flood the coordinator.
Evidence IDs make the result checkable.

mcq.q: Which is an organisational reason for multiple agents?
options: Agents owned by different teams or vendors must interoperate
mcq.why: Ownership boundaries can require separate agents.
distractors: Cost does not create a boundary.

mcq.q: A task is “summarise each of these 20 contracts, then compare”. What should you build?
options: A coordinator agent that discovers the plan
Parallel LLM calls in code, then a compare call
mcq.why: If the decomposition can be written in code, do that; it is cheaper and more predictable.
distractors: The task needs parallel calls, not more tools.

interview.q: When do multiple agents help, and when do they not?
covers: not for coupled or short tasks

interview.q: What does a multi-agent design cost compared with a single agent?
covers: several to many times the tokens

interview.q: Why is agreement between agents not proof of correctness?
A team wants a coordinator agent for a report whose steps are always the same. What do you suggest?
covers: keep agents for parts that vary

interview.q: How would you decide whether to split one agent into a billing agent and an account agent?
Your multi-agent research system costs 8× a single agent. How do you decide if it is worth it?
covers: quality gain on the same suite
use it only where it wins

interview.q: {company} wants an agent system that plans multi-city trips. Single agent, workflow or several agents? Justify.
interview.followUp: Where would you put human confirmation?

interview.q: Design a system that summarises complaints across tickets, sales notes and app reviews, each with different access rules.

mcq.q: Each of 6 sequential steps is 95% reliable. End to end is about…
mcq.why: 0.95⁶ ≈ 0.74; errors compound along the chain.

mcq.q: Two workers report different facts. How should the coordinator resolve it?
options: Use evidence, recency, source authority or a verification step, and surface unresolved conflicts
mcq.why: Resolve with rules and evidence; do not average conflicts away.

mcq.q: Each of 10 sequential steps is 90% reliable. What is end-to-end reliability?
Each of 6 steps is 95% reliable, and a verifier catches 50% of each step's errors. What is end-to-end reliability?
How does one worker's hallucination become a bigger problem?
options: It is always caught by synthesis
It becomes the coordinator's premise and the final report's headline
mcq.why: Errors propagate through the chain; evidence requirements break it.
distractors: Synthesis trusts worker inputs unless verified.

mcq.q: Choose all the defences against runaway loops.
options: Telling the evaluator to approve only perfect work
Global step, depth and spawn limits
A maximum number of critique rounds
mcq.why: Hard limits stop loops; “perfect” criteria cause them.
distractors: That is how the chapter's 14-round loop happened.

mcq.q: In the chapter's runaway critique example, what fixed it?
options: A rubric with concrete pass criteria, at most 2 revision rounds, then ship with notes for a human
mcq.why: Concrete criteria and a round limit end the loop.
distractors: Then there is nothing to evaluate.
A stronger evaluator still has no stopping rule.

mcq.q: When can coordination overhead exceed the useful work?
mcq.why: Briefs, summaries and synthesis cost tokens whatever the task size.
distractors: One worker has the least overhead.

mcq.q: A 2024 policy and a 2026 amendment conflict. Which rule should decide?
mcq.why: Source authority and recency rules resolve the conflict.

mcq.q: Agents send “please clarify” to each other repeatedly. Which control detects this?
mcq.why: Repeated messages are a loop signal.
distractors: More context does not stop the loop.

interview.q: How should a coordinator resolve conflicting worker outputs?
Why does reliability compound across steps, and what breaks the chain?
What causes runaway loops in multi-agent systems?
An evaluator agent rejected a report 14 times. How do you fix the system?
covers: ship with notes for a human

interview.q: Where would you add verification in a six-step chain, given a fixed budget?
covers: steps with highest error or impact

interview.q: A false fact from one worker appeared in an executive report. Trace and prevent it.
Two of {company}'s workers return different fares for the same route. Design the resolution rule and what the traveller sees.
covers: tell the traveller the price changed
interview.followUp: What if the live check fails?

interview.q: Design run-level guards for a platform where agents can spawn other agents.

mcq.q: A worker with broad credentials executes a lower-trust user's request. This is…
mcq.why: Pass the user's identity and narrow scopes at each hop instead.

mcq.q: When agent A asks agent B to act, whose permissions should apply by default?
options: The original user's, narrowed at each hop
mcq.why: Narrowing the user's rights at each hop prevents escalation.
distractors: A's rights may exceed the user's.
Service accounts may exceed the user's rights.

mcq.q: What does OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) do at each hop?
options: Exchanges the incoming token for a new one with narrower audience and scopes
mcq.why: Each hop can only reduce permissions; tokens are short-lived.
distractors: The user's identity must be kept.
Unchanged tokens are valid too broadly.

mcq.q: Why pass a user token rather than a user ID string?
options: Any agent could forge a plain ID string
mcq.why: A signed token proves who the user is; a string does not.

mcq.q: Where should the final access decision be made?
options: At the resource (tool or API), using the user's and the agent's identities
By the worker that holds the token
mcq.why: Agents never decide access for themselves.
distractors: The coordinator is not the authority.
The holder is not the authority.

mcq.q: What does an agent's own workload identity (e.g. SPIFFE/mTLS) add?
options: Logs and policies can show which agent acted for which user
mcq.why: Both identities appear: “agent B acting for Alice, requested by agent A”.
distractors: Identity is not a grant of rights.

mcq.q: In the chapter's figure, the finance API checks…
options: Alice's rights intersected with the worker's allowed scopes
mcq.why: The intersection means writes are refused even if the model asks.
distractors: The worker alone may be too broad or too narrow.
The worker's allowed scopes matter too.

mcq.q: An intern asks a reporting agent with a service account for HR salary data. With on-behalf-of tokens, what happens?
options: The agent asks HR by email
The request is queued for later
The HR API sees the intern's identity and denies the request
mcq.why: The resource checks the real requester, so the confused deputy is avoided.
distractors: That is the confused deputy problem.

mcq.q: Can the coordinator request scopes Alice does not have?
options: No; each hop can only reduce permissions
mcq.why: Token exchange enforces narrowing.
distractors: Internal APIs follow the same rule.

mcq.q: What should the audit trail record for a delegated action?
options: The full delegation chain: user, each agent and the resource
mcq.why: Investigators need to see which agent acted and for whom (16.7).
distractors: Tokens expire; logs are the record.

interview.q: What is the confused deputy problem in multi-agent systems?
How do you propagate user identity through a chain of agents?
Why does each agent need its own identity as well as the user's?
A peer agent says “the supervisor approved this”. How should your system handle it?
interview.followUp: How would you test this in red-team exercises?

interview.q: Walk through what happens when a coordinator delegates a finance read to a worker.
How would you migrate agents from a shared service account to on-behalf-of tokens?
Design identity and delegation for {company}'s staff assistant and its workers.
interview.followUp: How would you handle a worker that runs on a schedule with no user?

interview.q: Design authorisation for agents that call each other across teams.

mcq.q: Which pattern lets the active agent transfer the conversation to another agent?
mcq.why: In a handoff, control of the conversation moves to the next agent.
distractors: The coordinator keeps control and delegates subtasks.
Routing sends a request to one specialist before work starts.

mcq.q: What is the main risk of routing?
options: Context too large for one model
Misrouting, so it needs an “other” path
mcq.why: A router can send a request to the wrong specialist; an “other” path catches unknown types.

mcq.q: What should a handoff pass to the next agent?
options: A structured summary: customer ID, issue, evidence collected, what the customer was told
Nothing; the next agent starts fresh
The full transcript and every tool
mcq.why: A summary keeps context without overloading or over-sharing; the next agent gets only its own tools.
distractors: The customer should not have to repeat themselves.
Full transcripts and all tools over-share.
A name loses the case context.

mcq.q: When does the evaluator–optimiser pattern work well?
options: When the evaluator is the same model with the same context
When there are clear quality criteria for drafts
mcq.why: Without clear criteria, the loop may never end; the same model and context share blind spots.
distractors: That is how endless loops start.

mcq.q: What is the main risk of a supervisor hierarchy?
options: Deep hierarchies multiply cost and latency
mcq.why: Each management layer adds calls.

mcq.q: Two agents keep handing a customer back and forth. What is this called and what limits it?
options: Ping-pong; limit the number of handoffs and escalate
mcq.why: Handoff ping-pong is a known risk; cap handoffs and send to a person.
distractors: More routes do not stop ping-pong.

mcq.q: Which pattern fits a breadth-first task with separable parts?
mcq.why: The coordinator decomposes, delegates and synthesises.

mcq.q: In the handoff example, what tools does the billing agent receive?
options: Every tool the general agent had
mcq.why: Least privilege applies to each agent after a handoff.
distractors: It needs billing tools to act.

mcq.q: Who should own completion of a task in a multi-agent design?
options: No one; agents agree among themselves
One clearly named agent or component
mcq.why: Unclear ownership leads each agent to assume another will finish.

mcq.q: A coordinator in Harbor's design is plain code. Which pattern is that closest to?
mcq.why: The coordinator role can be code rather than a model when the plan is fixed.

interview.q: Describe the five multi-agent patterns and when to use each.
What should a handoff carry, and why not the whole transcript?
covers: evidence and what the customer was told

interview.q: What are the risks of evaluator–optimiser loops?
covers: need clear criteria and round limits

interview.q: Customers complain they repeat themselves after being transferred between agents. How do you fix it?
When would you choose routing over a coordinator?
How would you stop handoff ping-pong?
Design {assistant}'s path from a general question to a disputed charge, with the agents, tools and handoffs.
interview.followUp: What would the customer see at each step?

interview.q: Design a support system where several departments each own an agent.

mcq.q: What should a task brief include?
options: Objective, constraints, allowed tools, budget and output schema
mcq.why: A clear brief keeps workers focused and outputs combinable.
distractors: Workers need only the context relevant to them.
An objective alone leaves scope and format open.
Workers produce findings, not the final answer.

mcq.q: Six subtasks take 10, 20, 30, 10, 20 and 30 seconds. Ignoring overhead, how long does sequential execution take, and how long with all six in parallel?
mcq.why: Sequential is the sum (120 s); unlimited parallel waits for the slowest (30 s).

mcq.q: Parallel execution cuts wall-clock time. What happens to total token cost?
options: It drops to zero for workers
It stays the same or rises
It falls in proportion to parallelism
mcq.why: The same work is done, plus coordination overhead.

mcq.q: Why set a concurrency limit?
options: To protect rate limits and budgets
To reduce the number of subtasks
mcq.why: Unbounded parallel calls can hit provider rate limits and spend fast.

mcq.q: A coordinator delegates “research the market” to three workers. What is the likely result?
mcq.why: Vague delegation produces vague, overlapping outputs.

mcq.q: Synthesis must wait for the slowest worker unless…
options: You set a deadline and proceed with what returned
mcq.why: A deadline bounds latency; missing parts are marked.
distractors: Model size does not change worker latency.
More workers do not speed the slowest.

mcq.q: Which describes good decomposition?
options: Subtasks that each need the others' full detail
Subtasks as independent as possible, each with objective, scope, output format and stopping rule
mcq.why: Independence enables parallelism; clarity prevents overlap.
distractors: Tool count is not the unit of work.

mcq.q: What should synthesis keep so the final result is traceable?
mcq.why: Evidence links let reviewers check each claim.
distractors: Transcripts are too large for synthesis.

mcq.q: Workers each return 5,000-token raw dumps to a coordinator with a 32,000-token window and an 8,000-token system prompt and policy. How many workers fit before the window is full?
mcq.why: 32,000 − 8,000 = 24,000 tokens left; 24,000 / 5,000 = 4.8, so 4 full results fit. Condensed findings avoid this limit.

mcq.q: What context should a worker receive?
options: Only the context it needs for its subtask
mcq.why: Minimal context reduces cost and keeps data access least-privilege.
distractors: Independent workers do not need each other's results.
It needs constraints and inputs too.

interview.q: How do you decompose a task for workers?
What goes into a task brief?
What does parallel execution save and what does it not?
Your workers keep returning overlapping findings. How do you fix it?
interview.followUp: Where would you partition: by source, by topic or by time?

interview.q: The coordinator's context overflows when results come back. What do you change?
covers: evidence IDs instead of raw text

interview.q: How do you set a deadline for synthesis when one worker is often slow?
Design {company}'s trip-search fan-out: workers, concurrency limits per supplier, deadlines and synthesis.
interview.followUp: How would you handle a supplier that is down?

interview.q: Design a research system that reads 200 documents and returns a cited report.

mcq.q: What is a blackboard in multi-agent design?
options: A shared store that agents read and write
mcq.why: Shared state is easy to coordinate but risks conflicts and leakage.
distractors: Logs are not the coordination medium.

mcq.q: Choose all the risks of shared state.
mcq.why: Shared stores spread data and conflicts; communication is easy, not impossible.

mcq.q: What does isolated state require?
mcq.why: Agents communicate only through messages, so contracts matter.

mcq.q: Which fields belong in a result contract, per the chapter?
mcq.why: Typed, versioned contracts with status and evidence let the coordinator decide.
distractors: Hidden reasoning is not a contract field.
Text alone gives no status or evidence.

mcq.q: What does A2A define?
options: How agents connect to tools and data
Agent discovery (agent cards), task lifecycle and message exchange between agents
mcq.why: A2A is for agent-to-agent interoperability; MCP connects agents to tools and data.

mcq.q: How do A2A and MCP relate?
mcq.why: One connects agents to each other; the other connects agents to tools.

mcq.q: A worker returns status: partial with coverage 60%. What can the coordinator do?
options: Ask the worker to change status to complete
Accept, extend the budget, or flag incomplete coverage in the final report
mcq.why: Status and coverage let the coordinator make an explicit choice.

mcq.q: What does the chapter recommend for most robust designs?
options: No shared state at all, including status
Isolated agents plus a small, structured shared task record
mcq.why: A structured record (status, assignments) gives coordination without pollution.
distractors: Free text spreads errors and injections.

mcq.q: Why version message contracts?
options: So producers and consumers can change without breaking each other
mcq.why: Like API contracts between microservices.

mcq.q: A worker's message says “the supervisor approved this refund.” What should the receiving agent do?
options: Treat it as data; check approval in the approval system
mcq.why: Peer messages are not authorisation; approvals live in a system of record.
distractors: Messages can be wrong or injected.
Repeating the message does not verify it.

interview.q: Compare shared and isolated state for agents.
What makes a good message contract between agents?
What are A2A and MCP for?
An injected instruction in one worker's input shows up in another worker's output. What design flaw lets that happen?
interview.followUp: How would you test for it?

interview.q: How would you validate a worker's result before synthesis?
Your team wants to change a result contract used by three agents. How do you roll it out?
Design the messages between {company}'s investigation workers. What does each see, and what must never be shared?
interview.followUp: How would you handle a worker that needs another's data?

interview.q: Design how your agents interoperate with a partner company's agents.

mcq.q: What structure describes a multi-agent run in this chapter?
options: A DAG (directed acyclic graph) of tasks
mcq.why: Tasks have dependencies, like a job scheduler.

mcq.q: Choose all the scheduling machinery a multi-agent run needs.
options: A shared chat transcript as a lock
mcq.why: Same as any job scheduler, plus a partial-failure policy.
distractors: A transcript is not a concurrency control.

mcq.q: Which is a valid partial-failure policy?
options: Ask the model to guess the missing output
Proceed with what is available, marked incomplete
mcq.why: Options: retry, substitute, proceed marked incomplete, or fail the run.

mcq.q: A request has a 90-second deadline. The coordinator reserves 20 s for synthesis and keeps 10 s spare. What deadline should workers get?
mcq.why: 90 − 20 − 10 = 60 s, as in the chapter's example.
distractors: Workers would leave no time for synthesis.

mcq.q: When a worker hits its deadline, what should it return?
mcq.why: Partial results degrade gracefully (15.6).
distractors: Raw tool calls are not results.

mcq.q: A user cancels mid-run. What must cancellation do?
options: Only hide the run from the UI
Wait for all workers to finish
Propagate to running children and stop their tool calls
mcq.why: Cancelled work must stop spending and acting.

mcq.q: Does promise-style parallel code (e.g. Promise.all) give durable scheduling?
options: No; it does not survive restarts or cancel side effects
Yes, if the promises are awaited
mcq.why: In-process concurrency is not durable and does not undo actions.

mcq.q: Worker B times out after finishing its tool calls. The run proceeded and the answer was finalised. B's result arrives later. What should happen?
options: It cannot change the finalised answer; it can be logged or used in a follow-up
mcq.why: A late result must not alter a finalised answer without a new, explicit step.
distractors: Silent merges are the same problem.

mcq.q: Worker deadlines should be ___ than the deadline of the request that spawned them.
mcq.why: Deadlines flow down, each hop tighter, leaving time for later steps.
distractors: No time would remain for synthesis.
They must be derived from the parent.

mcq.q: Synthesis needs workers A, B and C. Worker C errors, the policy retries it once, and the retry succeeds. What happens next?
options: Synthesis runs with all three results, as normal
The run fails because C errored
Synthesis runs without C, marked incomplete
mcq.why: A successful retry satisfies the dependency; nothing is missing.
distractors: Only the failed task is retried.
The retry policy exists to recover from that error.
C's result is available after the retry.

interview.q: What scheduling features does a multi-agent run need?
How do deadlines flow through a coordinator and workers?
What are the options when one worker fails?
Users cancel a report but the API bill shows workers kept running. How do you fix it?
interview.followUp: What about side effects already done?

interview.q: How do you choose between proceeding with partial results and failing the whole run?
covers: risk of acting on incomplete data

interview.q: Your fan-out often waits on one slow worker. What do you do?
covers: move slow work out of the critical path

interview.q: Design {company}'s trip-planning DAG with timeouts, retries and a policy for a failed supplier.
interview.followUp: How does the traveller see a missing product?

interview.q: Design a durable scheduler for multi-agent runs that survives restarts.

mcq.q: What should a multi-agent design be compared against?
options: A well-prompted single agent and a fixed parallel workflow, on the same evaluation set
mcq.why: It must beat the strongest simple alternative at acceptable cost.
distractors: Weak baselines make any design look good.
That is an assumption to test.

mcq.q: What does pass^3 measure?
options: The share of tasks that succeed in all three of three runs
mcq.why: It measures reliability over repeated runs.
distractors: It needs all three runs to pass.

mcq.q: In the chapter's illustrative table, why does the parallel workflow ship?
options: It captures most of the gain; the team design adds 3 points for about 4× cost and much more latency
It has the lowest latency only because it is simpler
It has the highest task success
mcq.why: 78% vs 81% success, but $0.21 vs $0.88 per successful task and 31 s vs 112 s p95.
distractors: The decision rests on reliability per dollar.
The team design has higher success (81%).

mcq.q: A design costs $0.30 per task and succeeds on 60% of tasks. What is its cost per successful task?
What is an ablation in this context?
options: Removing or merging a component to see whether quality actually drops
mcq.why: For example, remove the evaluator or merge two workers.

mcq.q: In the chapter's ablation example, removing the critic changed success from 81% to 80%. What did the team do?
options: Kept the critic only for high-stakes reports, since the drop was within the confidence interval and cost fell 30%
mcq.why: A drop within noise did not justify 30% more cost and 35% more latency.
distractors: The data did not support it.

mcq.q: Choose all the component metrics the chapter suggests.
options: Number of agents in the design
mcq.why: Also how often conflicts are surfaced correctly.
distractors: Agent count is not a quality metric.

mcq.q: Why re-run the comparison when models improve?
options: A stronger single agent may close the gap
mcq.why: Model upgrades change the trade-off.
distractors: They are not wrong, just possibly outdated.

mcq.q: On a CPU laptop with one Ollama instance, why are wall-clock gains from parallel workers small?
options: Parallel calls queue behind each other unless OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL allows concurrency
Parallel code is not allowed in Python
mcq.why: The quality and token comparison is still valid.

mcq.q: Why is comparing an agent team with a deliberately weak single-agent baseline a problem?
options: It makes pass^k impossible to compute
Weak baselines are cheaper to run
It inflates the apparent gain of the team design
mcq.why: The design must beat the strongest simple alternative, not a straw man.
distractors: Cost is not the issue; the comparison is misleading.
They can, on the same suite.

interview.q: How do you evaluate whether a multi-agent design is worth it?
covers: success, pass^k, latency, cost per success

interview.q: What is an ablation, and why run one on an agent system?
Why measure cost per successful task rather than cost per task?
A team shows their agent team beats a single agent by 20 points. What questions do you ask?
interview.followUp: What would make you accept the result?

interview.q: Your multi-agent design is 3 points better at 4× the cost. How do you decide?
Which component metrics would you add to an agent evaluation, and why?
Plan {company}'s evaluation of single agent vs workflow vs agent team for trip planning.
interview.followUp: How would you split single-city and multi-city results?

interview.q: Design an evaluation harness that compares agent architectures continuously as models change.
